subtopics.title: Learning Concepts: Supervised, Unsupervised & Reinforcement Learning
subtopics.subtitle: What learning means (T, P, E), the learning agent and the three main paradigms

concepts.text: What Machine Learning Is

Machine learning is the branch of AI that builds systems which improve their behaviour from data or experience instead of being explicitly programmed for every case. Tom Mitchell's widely quoted definition: a program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. Learning is needed when the designer cannot anticipate every situation, when the environment changes over time, or when nobody knows how to write the solution down (for example, recognising handwriting).

rows: Classify e-mail as spam or not
A set of e-mails labelled spam / not spam
A database of labelled digit images
Average distance travelled before an error
Recorded images and steering commands of a human driver

concepts.text: The Learning Agent
Russell and Norvig divide a learning agent into four conceptual components:
items: Performance element: the part that selects external actions (this is the whole agent in the non-learning designs).
Critic: compares the agent's behaviour with a fixed performance standard and tells the learning element how well it is doing.
Learning element: uses the critic's feedback to make improvements to the performance element.
Problem generator: suggests exploratory actions that lead to new and informative experiences, even if they look sub-optimal in the short run.

concepts.text: The Three Main Paradigms

rows: Correct output (label) given for every training input
Classification, regression; decision trees, naive Bayes, neural networks, SVM, k-NN
Clustering (k-means, hierarchical), dimensionality reduction (PCA), association rules
Occasional scalar reward or penalty after actions
Game playing, robot control; Q-learning, policy search

concepts.text: In supervised learning the training set is a collection of input-output pairs (x, y) produced by an unknown function y = f(x); the learner searches a hypothesis space for a function h that approximates f. When the output is one of a finite set of discrete classes the task is classification (spam / not spam, disease A / B / C); when the output is a real number it is regression (predicting a house price or tomorrow's temperature).

Unsupervised learning looks for structure in unlabelled data. Clustering groups similar examples together: k-means picks k centroids, assigns each point to the nearest centroid, recomputes each centroid as the mean of its points and repeats until assignments stop changing. Dimensionality reduction such as principal component analysis (PCA) compresses many correlated features into a few components that keep most of the variance. Semi-supervised learning mixes a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one.
Reinforcement learning vocabulary:
items: Agent and environment: the agent observes a state s, takes an action a, and the environment returns a new state and a reward r.
Reward: a scalar signal saying how good the last step was; the agent never sees the correct action, only the consequence.
Policy π(s): the mapping from states to actions that the agent is trying to learn so as to maximise long-run (discounted) reward.
Value function: the expected total future reward from a state; Q(s, a) gives it for a state-action pair.
Exploration vs exploitation: trying new actions to learn more versus choosing the best-known action to collect reward.

concepts.plainText: Return G_t = r(t+1) + γ r(t+2) + γ² r(t+3) + ..., discount factor 0 ≤ γ < 1

concepts.text: Training, Testing and Generalisation

The real goal of learning is generalisation: performing well on new, unseen examples, not just on the training data. Data are therefore split into a training set (used to fit the model), often a validation set (used to tune choices such as tree depth), and a test set that is touched only once at the end to estimate true accuracy. k-fold cross-validation rotates the held-out part so every example is used for both training and testing.
Overfitting and underfitting:
items: Overfitting: the hypothesis is too complex and memorises noise; training error is very low but test error is high.
Underfitting: the hypothesis is too simple to capture the pattern; both training and test error are high.
Remedies for overfitting: more data, simpler models (Ockham's razor), pruning, regularisation, early stopping and cross-validation.
Inductive bias: the assumptions a learner uses to prefer one hypothesis over another consistent one; without some bias no generalisation is possible.

concepts.plainText: Accuracy = correctly classified test examples / total test examples

formulas.plainText: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
G_t = Σ γ^k r(t+k+1), the discounted return in reinforcement learning
MSE = (1/n) Σ (y_i − ŷ_i)², the usual regression error

notes.text: Decide the paradigm from the feedback: labels for every example means supervised, no labels means unsupervised, a delayed reward signal means reinforcement. Then decide classification vs regression from the output type: discrete class or real number.
A model is never judged on its training accuracy. Very high training accuracy with poor test accuracy is the textbook sign of overfitting, not of a good model.
In Mitchell's definition, E is the data or experience, T is what the program does and P is how success is scored. MCQs often give a scenario and ask which of the three a phrase describes.

formulas.title: Classification accuracy
formulas.plainText: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
formulas.description: Fraction of test examples a classifier labels correctly, from the confusion-matrix counts.

formulas.title: Discounted return
formulas.plainText: G_t = Σ γ^k r(t+k+1)
formulas.description: The long-run reward a reinforcement-learning agent tries to maximise; γ close to 1 values future rewards more.

formulas.title: Mean squared error
formulas.plainText: MSE = (1/n) Σ (y_i − ŷ_i)²
formulas.description: Average squared difference between true and predicted values, the standard loss for regression.

flashcards.front: State Mitchell's definition of machine learning.
flashcards.back: A program learns from experience E with respect to tasks T and performance measure P if its performance at T, measured by P, improves with E.

flashcards.front: What are the four components of a learning agent?
flashcards.back: Performance element (chooses actions), critic (gives feedback against a standard), learning element (makes improvements) and problem generator (suggests exploratory actions).
Both are supervised; classification predicts a discrete class label, regression predicts a continuous numeric value.

flashcards.front: What is a policy in reinforcement learning?
flashcards.back: A mapping π from states to actions; the agent learns the policy that maximises expected cumulative (discounted) reward.

questions.questionText: A spam filter improves its accuracy after being shown thousands of e-mails that users have marked as spam or not spam. In Mitchell's T-P-E definition of learning, the marked e-mails are:
options: The task T
The performance measure P
The experience E
The hypothesis space H
questions.explanation: E is the experience the program learns from, here the labelled e-mails. T is classifying e-mails and P is the fraction classified correctly.

questions.questionText: A bank wants to predict the exact loan amount (in rupees) a customer will request, using past customers whose requested amounts are known. This problem is best described as:
options: Supervised classification
Supervised regression
Unsupervised clustering
Reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Past examples carry the correct output, so it is supervised, and the output is a continuous number, so it is regression rather than classification.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes the feedback a reinforcement-learning agent receives?
options: The correct action for every state is supplied by a teacher
No feedback of any kind; it only groups similar states
A scalar reward or penalty that evaluates the consequences of its actions
The full transition model of the environment before learning starts
questions.explanation: A reinforcement-learning agent is never told the correct action; it receives only an evaluative scalar reward or penalty and must learn a policy that maximises long-run reward.

questions.questionText: A decision tree reaches 99% accuracy on its training set but only 62% on a separate test set. The most likely diagnosis and remedy are:
options: Overfitting; prune the tree or use a validation set to limit its growth
Underfitting; add more levels to the tree
The test set is too large; move test examples into training
The learning rate is too small; increase it
questions.explanation: A large gap between very high training accuracy and low test accuracy means the tree has memorised noise (overfitting). Pruning or limiting depth with a validation set improves generalisation.

subtopics.title: Inductive Learning: Decision Trees, Entropy & Information Gain
subtopics.subtitle: Learning a tree from examples with ID3, entropy, information gain and pruning

concepts.text: Inductive Learning

Inductive learning means generalising from specific examples to a general rule. Given a training set of pairs (x, f(x)) for an unknown target function f, the learner must find a hypothesis h from a hypothesis space H such that h approximates f, including on examples it has not seen. A hypothesis that agrees with all training examples is called consistent; when several are consistent, Ockham's razor prefers the simplest. Decision-tree learning is one of the simplest and most successful forms of inductive learning.
Decision Tree Representation
A decision tree classifies an example by testing attributes from the root down:
items: Each internal node tests one attribute (for example Outlook).
Each branch corresponds to one value of that attribute (Sunny, Overcast, Rain).
Each leaf assigns a class label (Play = Yes or No).
Every path from root to leaf is a conjunction of attribute tests, and the whole tree is a disjunction of these conjunctions, so a tree can represent any Boolean function of the attributes.

concepts.text: Entropy: Measuring Impurity

Entropy measures how mixed the class labels in a set S are. For two classes it is 0 when every example has the same class (a pure set) and reaches its maximum of 1 bit when the classes are split 50:50. With c classes the maximum is log2 c bits. By convention 0 log2 0 = 0.

concepts.plainText: H(S) = −Σ p_i log2 p_i, where p_i is the proportion of class i in S

concepts.text: Information Gain and the ID3 Algorithm

ID3 (Quinlan, 1986) grows the tree top-down and greedily: at each node it picks the attribute with the highest information gain, splits the data on it and recurses on each subset. It never backtracks, so it finds a small tree quickly but not necessarily the smallest possible one. C4.5, its successor, adds continuous attributes (threshold splits), handling of missing values, gain ratio and post-pruning.
Worked Example: PlayTennis (14 Days, 9 Yes / 5 No)

H(S) = -(9/14)log2(9/14) - (5/14)log2(5/14) = 0.940
Outlook: Sunny 2Y/3N (H=0.971), Overcast 4Y/0N (H=0), Rain 3Y/2N (H=0.971)
IG(Outlook) = 0.940 - (5/14)(0.971) - (4/14)(0) - (5/14)(0.971) = 0.247
Humidity: High 3Y/4N (H=0.985), Normal 6Y/1N (H=0.592)
IG(Humidity) = 0.940 - (7/14)(0.985) - (7/14)(0.592) = 0.152
Wind: Weak 6Y/2N (H=0.811), Strong 3Y/3N (H=1.0)
IG(Wind) = 0.940 - (8/14)(0.811) - (6/14)(1.0) = 0.048
IG(Temperature) = 0.029
=> Outlook has the highest gain and becomes the root; Overcast is a pure Yes leaf.
Overfitting, Pruning and Gain Ratio
A tree grown until every leaf is pure often overfits noisy data. Standard remedies:
items: Pre-pruning: stop growing early, for example when gain is below a threshold, a node has too few examples, or a chi-square test shows the split is not significant.

Post-pruning: grow the full tree, then replace subtrees by leaves when that does not reduce accuracy on a validation set (reduced-error pruning) or convert to rules and prune them (rule post-pruning in C4.5).
Gain ratio: information gain favours attributes with many values (an ID number splits every example into its own pure leaf); C4.5 divides the gain by the split information to correct this bias.
Gini index: an alternative impurity measure 1 − Σ p_i² used by CART.

concepts.plainText: GainRatio(S, A) = IG(S, A) / SplitInfo(S, A), SplitInfo = −Σ (|S_v|/|S|) log2(|S_v|/|S|)

formulas.plainText: H(S) = −Σ p_i log2 p_i
IG(S, A) = H(S) − Σ (|S_v| / |S|) H(S_v)
Gini(S) = 1 − Σ p_i²

notes.text: Memorise a few entropy values to save time: H(1/2, 1/2) = 1, H(1/4, 3/4) = 0.811, H(1/3, 2/3) = 0.918, H(2/5, 3/5) = 0.971, H(9/14, 5/14) = 0.940. A pure set always has entropy 0.
Information gain is the parent entropy minus the WEIGHTED average of the child entropies. Forgetting the weights |S_v|/|S| is the most common calculation mistake.
ID3 is greedy hill-climbing in the space of trees with no backtracking; it prefers shorter trees with high-gain attributes near the root, which is its inductive bias.

formulas.title: Entropy
formulas.plainText: H(S) = −Σ p_i log2 p_i
formulas.description: Impurity of a set of examples; 0 for a pure set and 1 bit for an even two-class split.

formulas.title: Information gain
formulas.plainText: IG(S, A) = H(S) − Σ (|S_v| / |S|) H(S_v)
formulas.description: Expected reduction in entropy from splitting on attribute A; ID3 splits on the attribute with the largest value.

formulas.title: Split information
formulas.plainText: SplitInfo(S, A) = −Σ (|S_v|/|S|) log2(|S_v|/|S|)
formulas.description: Denominator of C4.5's gain ratio, large for attributes with many values, which penalises them.

formulas.title: Gini index
formulas.plainText: Gini(S) = 1 − Σ p_i²
formulas.description: Alternative impurity measure used by CART; 0 for a pure set and 0.5 for an even two-class split.

flashcards.front: How does ID3 choose the attribute at each node?
flashcards.back: It computes the information gain of every remaining attribute on the current examples and splits on the one with the highest gain, greedily and without backtracking.

flashcards.front: What is the entropy of the PlayTennis set with 9 Yes and 5 No?
Why does C4.5 use gain ratio instead of plain information gain?
flashcards.back: Information gain is biased towards attributes with many values (such as an ID); dividing by split information penalises such attributes.
Replacing a subtree by a leaf with its majority class whenever doing so does not lower accuracy on a separate validation set.

questions.questionText: A node in a decision tree contains 8 training examples: 6 positive and 2 negative. What is the entropy of this node (to 3 decimal places)?
A set S has 4 positive and 4 negative examples. Attribute A splits it into A = x (3 positive, 1 negative) and A = y (1 positive, 3 negative). What is IG(S, A)?
questions.explanation: H(S) = 1. Each child has entropy H(3/4, 1/4) = 0.811 and weight 4/8, so the weighted child entropy is 0.811. IG = 1 − 0.811 = 0.189.

questions.questionText: When a 'Customer ID' attribute (unique for every example) is offered to ID3, it gets the highest information gain. Which modification in C4.5 is designed to counter this bias?
options: Using the Gini index instead of entropy
Dividing information gain by split information (gain ratio)
Choosing the attribute with the lowest information gain
Splitting only on binary attributes
questions.explanation: A unique ID splits every example into its own pure leaf, so its gain equals H(S). Gain ratio divides by split information, which is very large for such many-valued attributes.

questions.questionText: In reduced-error pruning of a decision tree, a subtree is replaced by a leaf when:
options: The subtree has more than two branches
The information gain at its root is exactly zero on the training set
Its depth exceeds log2 of the number of attributes
Replacing it does not reduce classification accuracy on a separate validation set
questions.explanation: Reduced-error pruning uses held-out validation data: a node is pruned to its majority class if the pruned tree performs no worse on the validation set, which removes branches that only fit noise.

subtopics.title: Statistical Learning: The Naive Bayes Model
subtopics.subtitle: Bayes' theorem as a classifier, the independence assumption, smoothing and spam filtering

concepts.text: Statistical Learning

Statistical learning treats learning as probabilistic inference: from data we estimate probabilities, then classify a new example by choosing the class that is most probable given its features. The naive Bayes model is the simplest and one of the most widely used statistical learners. It is a generative model: it learns how each class generates features, P(x | c), and the class priors P(c), and then inverts them with Bayes' theorem.

concepts.plainText: P(c | x) = P(x | c) P(c) / P(x)

concepts.text: Terms in Bayes' theorem for classification:
items: Prior P(c): how common class c is before seeing the example (fraction of training examples in c).
Likelihood P(x | c): how probable the observed features are if the class is c.
Evidence P(x): the same for every class, so it can be ignored when only the most probable class is wanted.
Posterior P(c | x): the probability of the class after seeing the features; the maximum a posteriori (MAP) class is chosen.

concepts.text: The Naive Conditional-Independence Assumption

Estimating P(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n | c) directly needs an entry for every combination of feature values, which is impossible with realistic data. Naive Bayes assumes that the features are conditionally independent of each other given the class, so the joint likelihood factorises into a product of one-feature terms. As a Bayesian network, the class is the single parent of every feature node. The assumption is rarely exactly true, yet the classifier often works well because only the ranking of classes matters, not the exact probabilities.

concepts.plainText: c_NB = argmax over c of P(c) × Π P(x_i | c)

concepts.text: Worked Example: Should We Play Tennis?

Using the standard 14-day PlayTennis data (9 Yes, 5 No), classify a new day with Outlook = Sunny, Temperature = Cool, Humidity = High, Wind = Strong. The table lists the counts estimated from the training data.
Zero Counts and Laplace Smoothing

If a feature value never occurs with a class in training, its estimated probability is 0 and the whole product becomes 0, no matter how strongly the other features point to that class. Laplace (add-one) smoothing adds 1 to every count and adds the number of possible values k to the denominator, so no probability is ever exactly zero. A more general m-estimate adds m virtual examples distributed according to a prior p.

concepts.latex: P(x_i = v \mid c) = \frac{\text{count}(x_i = v, c) + 1}{\text{count}(c) + k}
concepts.plainText: P(x_i = v | c) = (count(x_i = v, c) + 1) / (count(c) + k), k = number of possible values

concepts.text: Practical points and applications:
items: Log probabilities: multiplying many small numbers underflows, so implementations add log P(x_i | c) instead of multiplying.
Continuous features: modelled with a Gaussian per class using the class mean and variance (Gaussian naive Bayes).
Spam filtering: words are features; P(word | spam) and P(word | ham) are estimated from labelled mail (multinomial or Bernoulli naive Bayes).
Other uses: document and sentiment classification, medical diagnosis, recommendation; training is a single counting pass, so it is very fast and works with small data sets.

formulas.latex: P(c \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} \mid c) P(c)}{\sum_{c'} P(\mathbf{x} \mid c') P(c')}
formulas.plainText: P(c | x) = P(x | c)P(c) / Σ P(x | c')P(c')
c_NB = argmax P(c) Π P(x_i | c)
P(v | c) = (n_vc + 1) / (n_c + k), Laplace smoothing

notes.text: For a numeric naive Bayes MCQ: multiply prior by each feature likelihood for every class, compare the products, and only divide by their sum if the question asks for an actual posterior probability.
Naive Bayes assumes independence of the features GIVEN the class, not that features are independent in general, and not that the class is independent of the features.
Because the evidence P(x) is the same for all classes, argmax of P(c | x) equals argmax of P(x | c)P(c); this is the MAP decision rule.

formulas.title: Bayes' theorem
formulas.plainText: P(c | x) = P(x | c) P(c) / P(x)
formulas.description: Converts the class-conditional likelihood and prior into the posterior probability of the class.

formulas.title: Naive Bayes decision rule
formulas.plainText: c_NB = argmax P(c) Π P(x_i | c)
formulas.description: Chooses the class with the largest prior times product of per-feature likelihoods, assuming conditional independence.

formulas.title: Laplace smoothing
formulas.description: Adds one to every count so unseen feature values never get zero probability; k is the number of possible values.

flashcards.front: What independence assumption does naive Bayes make?
flashcards.back: All features are conditionally independent of one another given the class, so P(x_1..x_n | c) = Π P(x_i | c).

flashcards.front: What problem does Laplace smoothing solve?
flashcards.back: The zero-frequency problem: a feature value unseen with a class would give probability 0 and wipe out the whole product; adding 1 to counts prevents this.

flashcards.front: Why do naive Bayes implementations sum log probabilities?
flashcards.back: Multiplying many probabilities smaller than 1 causes floating-point underflow; summing logs gives the same argmax safely.

questions.questionText: 30% of incoming e-mails are spam. The word 'lottery' appears in 60% of spam e-mails and in 10% of non-spam e-mails. An e-mail contains 'lottery'. What is the probability it is spam?

Training data: 10 e-mails, 4 spam and 6 ham. 'offer' appears in 3 spam and 1 ham; 'meeting' appears in 1 spam and 4 ham. A new e-mail contains 'offer' but not 'meeting'. Using naive Bayes (no smoothing), P(spam | e-mail) is approximately:

In a naive Bayes text classifier, the word 'refund' never appears in 20 training documents of class C, and the attribute has k = 10 possible values. With Laplace (add-one) smoothing, the estimate of P(refund | C) is:
questions.explanation: Laplace estimate = (0 + 1) / (20 + 10) = 1/30 ≈ 0.033, small but non-zero, so one unseen value no longer forces the class probability to 0.

questions.questionText: A naive Bayes classifier with 5,000 word features often returns a score of exactly 0.0 for every class on long documents, even with smoothing. The standard fix is to:
options: Drop the class prior from the calculation
Replace the product of probabilities by a sum of log probabilities
Assume all features are dependent
Use the evidence P(x) as the decision score
questions.explanation: Multiplying thousands of small probabilities underflows floating-point arithmetic. Because log is monotonic, maximising log P(c) + Σ log P(x_i | c) gives the same class without underflow.

subtopics.title: Fuzzy Learning & Fuzzy Inference Systems
subtopics.subtitle: Fuzzy sets, membership functions, fuzzy rules, Mamdani vs Sugeno and defuzzification

concepts.text: Crisp Sets vs Fuzzy Sets

In a classical (crisp) set an element either belongs (membership 1) or does not (membership 0). Lotfi Zadeh introduced fuzzy sets in 1965 so that an element can belong partially, with a membership degree μ_A(x) anywhere in [0, 1]. A temperature of 28 °C might be 0.8 'warm' and 0.3 'hot' at the same time. Fuzzy logic lets systems reason with the vague, linguistic knowledge humans use, and 'fuzzy learning' refers to building or tuning such membership functions and rules from data (for example with neuro-fuzzy systems such as ANFIS).
Membership Functions

rows: Rises linearly from a to peak 1 at b, falls to 0 at c; simple and common
Rises a to b, flat at 1 from b to c, falls c to d; models a range of full membership

concepts.plainText: Triangular: μ(x) = max(min((x − a)/(b − a), (c − x)/(c − b)), 0)

concepts.text: Fuzzy Operations, Linguistic Variables and Hedges
Standard (Zadeh) fuzzy set operations:
items: Intersection / AND: μ(A ∩ B)(x) = min(μ_A(x), μ_B(x)).
Union / OR: μ(A ∪ B)(x) = max(μ_A(x), μ_B(x)).
Complement / NOT: μ(not A)(x) = 1 − μ_A(x).
Unlike crisp sets, A ∩ not A need not be empty and A ∪ not A need not be the universe: the laws of contradiction and excluded middle fail.
Alternative operators: algebraic product a·b for AND and probabilistic sum a + b − ab for OR.

concepts.text: A linguistic variable takes words rather than numbers as values: the variable Temperature may take the terms Cold, Warm and Hot, each defined by a fuzzy set over degrees Celsius. Hedges modify terms: 'very' concentrates a set (μ²), 'somewhat' or 'more or less' dilates it (√μ), and 'not' takes the complement. If μ_Warm(x) = 0.8 then μ_VeryWarm(x) = 0.64.
Fuzzy Rules and the Inference Pipeline

Fuzzy inference system (FIS) steps:
1. Fuzzification: map crisp inputs to membership degrees of each term
2. Rule evaluation: apply IF-THEN rules; AND = min, OR = max gives firing strength
3. Implication: clip (min) or scale (product) each rule's output set by its strength
4. Aggregation: combine all rule outputs into one fuzzy set (usually max)
5. Defuzzification: convert the aggregated set into one crisp output value
Example rule: IF temperature is Warm AND humidity is High THEN fan is Fast

rows: Crisp function z = ax + by + c or a constant
Computationally efficient, suits optimisation and adaptive (ANFIS) tuning

concepts.text: Defuzzification Methods
Common ways to turn the aggregated fuzzy output into a crisp number:
items: Centroid (centre of gravity): the balance point of the area under the aggregated membership curve; the most widely used.
Mean of maxima (MOM): the average of the x values at which the membership is highest.
Smallest / largest of maxima: the first or last x where the maximum occurs.
Bisector: the x value that divides the area into two equal halves.
Weighted average: used in Sugeno systems, Σ w_i z_i / Σ w_i.

concepts.plainText: Discrete centroid z* = Σ μ(z_i) z_i / Σ μ(z_i)

concepts.text:
Input 28 °C: Warm = tri(20,30,40) -> 0.8, Hot = tri(25,35,45) -> 0.3
R1: IF Warm THEN speed Medium (50)   strength 0.8
R2: IF Hot  THEN speed Fast   (80)   strength 0.3
Sugeno weighted average = (0.8x50 + 0.3x80) / (0.8 + 0.3) = 64 / 1.1 = 58.2
Mamdani, sampled aggregated set: z = 30, 50, 70, 90 with mu = 0.5, 0.8, 0.3, 0.3
Centroid = (15 + 40 + 21 + 27) / (0.5 + 0.8 + 0.3 + 0.3) = 103 / 1.9 = 54.2
Mean of maxima: highest mu 0.8 occurs only at z = 50 -> MOM = 50

formulas.plainText: AND = min(μA, μB), OR = max(μA, μB), NOT = 1 − μA
Centroid z* = ∫ μ(z) z dz / ∫ μ(z) dz
Gaussian membership μ(x) = exp(−(x − c)² / (2σ²))

notes.text: Remember the pipeline order: fuzzification, rule evaluation (with implication), aggregation, defuzzification. Mamdani outputs are fuzzy sets that need defuzzification; Sugeno outputs are crisp functions combined by a weighted average.
Fuzzy membership is not probability. μ = 0.8 means 28 °C is warm to degree 0.8, not that there is an 80% chance it is warm; memberships of different terms need not sum to 1.
For triangular MFs, compute membership from the nearer slope: on the rising side (x − a)/(b − a), on the falling side (c − x)/(c − b).

formulas.title: Fuzzy AND, OR, NOT
formulas.plainText: AND = min, OR = max, NOT = 1 − μ
formulas.description: Zadeh's standard operators for intersection, union and complement of fuzzy sets.

formulas.title: Triangular membership
formulas.plainText: μ(x) = max(min((x − a)/(b − a), (c − x)/(c − b)), 0)
formulas.description: Membership rising from a to a peak of 1 at b and falling to 0 at c.

formulas.title: Discrete centroid
formulas.plainText: z* = Σ μ(z_i) z_i / Σ μ(z_i)
formulas.description: Centre-of-gravity defuzzification over sampled output values.

formulas.title: Sugeno weighted average
formulas.plainText: z = Σ w_i z_i / Σ w_i
formulas.description: Crisp output of a Sugeno FIS, where w_i is each rule's firing strength and z_i its crisp consequent.

flashcards.front: What is the main difference between Mamdani and Sugeno inference?
flashcards.back: Mamdani rule consequents are fuzzy sets that are aggregated and defuzzified; Sugeno consequents are crisp functions (linear or constant) combined by a weighted average.

flashcards.front: List the steps of a fuzzy inference system.
flashcards.back: Fuzzification, rule evaluation (with implication), aggregation of rule outputs, and defuzzification.

flashcards.front: If μ_Tall(x) = 0.8, what is μ for 'very tall' and 'somewhat tall'?

questions.questionText: The fuzzy set 'Warm' has a triangular membership function with a = 20 °C, b = 30 °C (peak) and c = 40 °C. What is the membership degree of 34 °C in 'Warm'?
questions.explanation: 34 °C is on the falling side, so μ = (c − x)/(c − b) = (40 − 34)/(40 − 30) = 0.6.

questions.questionText: For an element x, μ_A(x) = 0.7 and μ_B(x) = 0.4. Using the standard fuzzy operators, what is the membership of x in (NOT A) OR B?
The aggregated output of a Mamdani FIS is sampled at z = 10, 20, 30, 40 with memberships 0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 0.4. What is the crisp output using the (discrete) centroid method?
In a Sugeno (Takagi-Sugeno-Kang) fuzzy inference system, the consequent of each rule is:
options: A crisp function of the inputs, such as z = ax + by + c or a constant
A fuzzy set that must be clipped and aggregated before centroid defuzzification
A probability distribution over output classes
Another IF-THEN rule evaluated recursively
questions.explanation: Sugeno rules have crisp (linear or constant) consequents, and the final output is the firing-strength-weighted average, so no separate fuzzy-set defuzzification is needed as in Mamdani.

subtopics.title: Genetic Algorithms: Encoding, Selection, Operators & Fitness
subtopics.subtitle: The GA cycle, encodings, fitness, roulette/tournament/rank selection, crossover and mutation

concepts.text: What a Genetic Algorithm Is

A genetic algorithm (GA), introduced by John Holland in the 1970s, is a stochastic search and optimisation method inspired by Darwinian natural selection. It keeps a population of candidate solutions (chromosomes), each made of genes, and repeatedly selects the fitter ones to produce offspring by crossover and mutation. Over generations the population evolves towards better solutions. GAs need only a way to score solutions, not gradients, so they suit large, discontinuous or poorly understood search spaces such as scheduling, timetabling and design optimisation.

Genetic algorithm:
1. Choose an encoding; create a random initial population of N chromosomes
2. Evaluate the fitness f(x) of every chromosome
3. Repeat until the termination condition holds:
   a. Selection: choose parents with probability favouring high fitness
   b. Crossover: with probability pc, recombine pairs of parents
   c. Mutation: with small probability pm, alter each gene
   d. Evaluate offspring; form the next generation (optionally keep elites)
4. Return the best chromosome found
Encoding Schemes

rows: Knapsack (take item or not), integer x coded in bits
Genetic programming: evolving programs or expressions

concepts.text: Fitness Function

The fitness function measures how good a chromosome is and is the only link between the GA and the problem. For maximisation it can be the objective itself; for minimisation it is transformed, for example f = 1/(1 + cost). Constraint violations are usually handled with penalty terms. Roulette-wheel selection requires non-negative fitness values, so objectives may need to be shifted or scaled.
Selection Methods
Selection decides which chromosomes become parents:
items: Roulette wheel (fitness-proportionate): each chromosome gets a slice of the wheel proportional to its fitness, p_i = f_i / Σ f_j.
Tournament: pick k chromosomes at random and take the fittest; larger k gives stronger selection pressure. It works with negative fitness and needs no global sum.
Rank: sort by fitness and assign selection probability by rank, not raw fitness; this stops one 'super-individual' dominating early and keeps pressure when fitnesses are similar.
Elitism: copy the best one or few chromosomes unchanged into the next generation so the best solution is never lost.

concepts.plainText: p_i = f_i / Σ f_j; expected copies = N p_i = f_i / average fitness

concepts.text: Crossover and Mutation

P1 = 11010110   P2 = 01101001
Single-point after bit 3: 110|10110, 011|01001 -> 11001001, 01110110
Two-point after bits 2 and 5: 11|010|110, 01|101|001 -> 11101110, 01010001
Uniform, mask 10110010 (1 = take from P1 for child 1):
  C1 = 11011011   C2 = 01100100
Bit-flip mutation at bit 4 of 11101110 -> 11111110
Swap mutation (permutation) 3 1 5 2 4 -> swap pos 2,4 -> 3 2 5 1 4

Crossover (recombination) exploits good building blocks by combining parts of two parents; it is applied with a high probability pc, typically 0.6 to 0.9. Mutation explores by making small random changes, preventing premature convergence and restoring lost gene values; it is applied with a low probability pm per gene, typically 0.001 to 0.05 (often about 1/L for chromosome length L). Permutation encodings need special operators such as order crossover (OX), partially mapped crossover (PMX), and swap or inversion mutation so offspring remain valid permutations.
GA parameters and termination:
items: Population size N: typically 20 to a few hundred; too small loses diversity, too large wastes evaluations.
Crossover rate pc and mutation rate pm: balance exploitation against exploration.
Number of generations and selection pressure (tournament size, elitism count).
Termination: a fixed number of generations, a satisfactory fitness reached, no improvement for several generations (stagnation), or a time or evaluation budget exhausted.

formulas.plainText: Roulette-wheel selection probability p_i = f_i / Σ f_j
Expected number of bit flips per generation = N × L × pm
Fitness for a minimisation problem f(x) = 1 / (1 + cost(x))

notes.text: For a roulette-wheel MCQ, add all fitness values first, then divide the chosen chromosome's fitness by the total. Expected copies in the mating pool = N × p_i = f_i / average fitness.
Do not use plain bit-flip mutation or single-point crossover on permutation (TSP) chromosomes: they produce duplicate or missing cities. Use order/PMX crossover and swap or inversion mutation.
Selection and crossover exploit what the population already knows; mutation explores new regions. Elitism guarantees the best-so-far fitness never decreases between generations.

formulas.title: Roulette-wheel probability
formulas.plainText: p_i = f_i / Σ f_j
formulas.description: Chance that chromosome i is picked in one spin of fitness-proportionate selection.

formulas.title: Expected copies
formulas.plainText: n_i = N p_i = f_i / average fitness
formulas.description: Expected number of copies of chromosome i in a mating pool of size N under roulette selection.

formulas.title: Expected mutations
formulas.plainText: Expected bit flips = N × L × pm
formulas.description: Average number of genes mutated per generation for population N, chromosome length L and mutation rate pm.

flashcards.front: What is elitism in a genetic algorithm?
flashcards.back: Copying the best chromosome(s) of the current generation unchanged into the next, so the best solution found is never lost.

flashcards.front: Why is rank selection sometimes preferred to roulette-wheel selection?
flashcards.back: It uses ranks instead of raw fitness, so one very fit individual cannot dominate early (premature convergence) and pressure remains when fitnesses are close.

flashcards.front: Which encoding suits the travelling salesman problem?
flashcards.back: Permutation encoding, where each chromosome is an ordering of cities, used with order/PMX crossover and swap or inversion mutation.

flashcards.front: Name four common GA termination conditions.
flashcards.back: Maximum generations reached, target fitness achieved, no improvement for several generations, or time/evaluation budget exhausted.

questions.questionText: A GA maximises f(x) = x² with a population of four 5-bit strings encoding x = 13, 24, 8 and 19. Using roulette-wheel selection, what is the probability of selecting the string for x = 24 in one spin?
questions.explanation: Fitnesses are 169, 576, 64 and 361, totalling 1170. p = 576 / 1170 ≈ 0.49.

questions.questionText: Parents 11001011 and 00110110 undergo single-point crossover with the cut after the 5th bit. The two offspring are:
questions.explanation: Keep the first 5 bits and swap the tails: 11001|011 and 00110|110 give 11001 + 110 = 11001110 and 00110 + 011 = 00110011.

questions.questionText: A binary GA has a population of 20 chromosomes, each 10 bits long, and a bit-flip mutation rate of 0.01 per bit. On average, how many bits are mutated per generation?
questions.explanation: Expected flips = N × L × pm = 20 × 10 × 0.01 = 2.

questions.questionText: A GA for the travelling salesman problem encodes each tour as a permutation of city numbers. Which pair of operators keeps every offspring a valid tour?
options: Single-point crossover and bit-flip mutation
Order crossover (OX) and swap mutation
Uniform crossover and Gaussian mutation
Arithmetic crossover and creep mutation
questions.explanation: Order crossover preserves relative city order without duplicates, and swapping two cities keeps a permutation. Plain single-point or uniform crossover and bit-flip create repeated or missing cities.
